claim: A positive interspecific relationship between abundance and distribution (abundance-occupancy relationships or AORs) is considered one of the most general and robust patterns in ecology.
source: A positive interspecific relationship between abundance and distribution –abundance-occupancy relationships (AORs) – is considered one of the most general and robust patterns in ecology (Blackburn et al., 2006; Gaston, 1996; Gaston et al., 1997b; Ten Caten et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple scholarly works that have established this pattern in the literature.

claim: The AOR is sometimes referred to as a macroecological law.
source: Sometimes referred to as a macroecological law (Gaston and Blackburn, 1999b; Lawton, 1999), the AOR asserts that empirically locally abundant species tend to be widely distributed, and conversely, locally rare species tend to be geographically restricted in their range.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to scholarly works that have characterized AOR as a macroecological law.

claim: Locally abundant species tend to be widely distributed, and locally rare species tend to be geographically restricted in their range.
source: Sometimes referred to as a macroecological law (Gaston and Blackburn, 1999b; Lawton, 1999), the AOR asserts that empirically locally abundant species tend to be widely distributed, and conversely, locally rare species tend to be geographically restricted in their range.
evidence: This claim represents the core assertion of AOR and is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The mechanism driving the AOR relationship was never proven and remains unresolved.
source: The mechanism driving this relationship was never proven, and it remains unresolved why species distribution should affect per-unit-area abundance (or vice versa).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the state of knowledge regarding AOR mechanisms.

claim: The existence of a pervasive AOR has underpinned many practical applications in ecology and conservation.
source: Nonetheless, the existence of a pervasive AOR has underpinned many practical applications in ecology and conservation (Gaston, 1999a), e.g., setting harvest rates for fisheries (Swain and Morin, 1996), managing invasive species by restricting expansion rather than local elimination, and identifying species at high risk of extinction in biodiversity inventories such as the IUCN Red List Criteria (Gaston et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to works describing practical applications of AOR.

claim: AOR has been used for setting harvest rates for fisheries.
source: Nonetheless, the existence of a pervasive AOR has underpinned many practical applications in ecology and conservation (Gaston, 1999a), e.g., setting harvest rates for fisheries (Swain and Morin, 1996), managing invasive species by restricting expansion rather than local elimination, and identifying species at high risk of extinction in biodiversity inventories such as the IUCN Red List Criteria (Gaston et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific application in fisheries management.

claim: Many plausible biological mechanisms have been proposed for AORs, yet none has unequivocal support.
source: Many plausible biological mechanisms have been proposed for AORs, yet none of them has unequivocal support (Gaston et al., 1997b; Ten Caten et al., 2022; Wilson, 2008; Borregaard and Rahbek, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple review works discussing proposed mechanisms.

claim: A spatially explicit neutral model of biodiversity and biogeography can generate AORs.
source: Among all mechanisms, it is noteworthy that a spatially explicit neutral model of biodiversity and biogeography can generate AORs (Bell, 2001; Hubbell, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical works on neutral models.

claim: The neutral model can produce a positive correlation between species range and their per-unit-area local and total global abundance.
source: Specifically, this macroecological 'null' model can produce a positive correlation between species range (or occupancy) and their per-unit-area local, as well as total global abundance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the discussion of neutral theory predictions in the context of the preceding citation.

claim: Neutral theory may provide a biological null model for community and macroecology.
source: This observation, in turn, supports the utility of neutral theory as a null model of community and macroecology (Bell, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to theoretical work on neutral theory.

claim: Sampling bias can create AORs because locally rare species are more likely to be missed, resulting in an underestimation of range size or occupancy.
source: Indeed, sampling bias can create AORs because locally rare species are more likely to be missed, resulting in an underestimation of range size or occupancy, thereby generating a positive relationship (Borregaard and Rahbek, 2010; Bock and Ricklefs, 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to works discussing sampling bias as a mechanism.

claim: The sampling explanation for AORs has long been discarded as a plausible mechanism.
source: Yet, this sampling explanation has long been discarded as a plausible mechanism leading to observed patterns (Gaston, 1996; Gaston et al., 1997b; Blackburn and Gaston, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to works that have dismissed sampling bias as an explanation.

claim: A meta-analysis of 279 effect sizes found an overall effect of r=0.58 (or Fisher's transformation: Zr = 0.66) for AORs in 2006.
source: This is because of substantial empirical evidence for positive interspecific relationships, including a meta-analysis of 279 effect sizes with an overall effect of r=0.58 (or its Fisher's transformation: Zr = 0.66) in 2006 (Blackburn et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific meta-analysis with quantitative results.

claim: A large amount of variation exists in empirical patterns of AORs, including strikingly negative relationships.
source: Nonetheless, a large amount of variation does exist in empirical patterns of AORs, including strikingly negative relationships (Wilson, 2008; Päivinen et al., 2005; Komonen et al., 2009; Kotiaho et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing variation in AOR patterns.

claim: Some of the observed heterogeneity in AORs is likely due to different aspects of sampling, such as the number of species and spatial and temporal coverage.
source: Some of the observed heterogeneity is likely to be due to different aspects of sampling, such as the number of species and spatial and temporal coverage (Gaston et al., 1997b; Ten Caten et al., 2022; Wilson, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to works discussing sources of heterogeneity in AOR studies.

claim: Confirmation bias and publication bias are widespread in ecological studies.
source: Although both biases are widespread, including in ecological studies (Holman et al., 2015; van Wilgenburg and Elgar, 2013; Yang et al., 2023), no studies so far systematically considered or quantified both biases in the context of AORs (Blackburn et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to meta-research studies on bias in ecology.

claim: No studies have systematically considered or quantified confirmation bias and publication bias in the context of AORs.
source: Although both biases are widespread, including in ecological studies (Holman et al., 2015; van Wilgenburg and Elgar, 2013; Yang et al., 2023), no studies so far systematically considered or quantified both biases in the context of AORs (Blackburn et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the state of research on bias in AOR studies.

claim: The study uses data from eBird, a global citizen science dataset aimed at counting birds.
source: Here, we use data from eBird – a global citizen science dataset aimed at counting birds – to quantify the relationship between local-scale (and global-scale) abundance and global-scale range size as a proxy for occupancy (AOR).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data source used in the study.

claim: Large citizen science datasets collected for non-hypothesis-driven purposes have the advantage of avoiding biases such as confirmation and publication bias.
source: Large citizen science datasets collected for non-hypothesis-driven purposes are not random samples (see Callaghan et al., 2017), but they have the advantage of avoiding biases such as confirmation and publication bias.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the nature of citizen science data collection and is supported by a citation.

claim: The eBird dataset allows estimation of heterogeneity due to sampling intensity.
source: Also, using the eBird dataset allows us to estimate heterogeneity due to sampling intensity (e.g. the duration of a sampling event directly influences the number of species recorded).
evidence: This claim is based on the characteristics of the eBird dataset and logical inference about what can be measured.

claim: Increases in species richness and sampling duration are predicted to reduce the magnitude of AORs.
source: Specifically, we can quantify how AOR will change in relation to increases in species richness and sampling duration, both of which are predicted to reduce the magnitude of AORs (Gaston et al., 1997b; Ten Caten et al., 2022; Komonen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to works predicting these effects.

claim: Global range size should be relatively stable compared to local range sizes.
source: For occupancy, we use global range size not only because global range size should be relatively stable – 'local' range sizes for one species could vary dramatically – but also because different types of occupancy measures were deemed to contribute less to the observation heterogeneity (Wilson, 2011; Steenweg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the stability of global versus local measures and is supported by citations.

claim: Different types of occupancy measures contribute less to observation heterogeneity.
source: For occupancy, we use global range size not only because global range size should be relatively stable – 'local' range sizes for one species could vary dramatically – but also because different types of occupancy measures were deemed to contribute less to the observation heterogeneity (Wilson, 2011; Steenweg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on occupancy measures.

claim: The study conducted a meta-analysis of 16,562,995 correlations from eBird checklists.
source: First, we carry out the largest known meta-analysis by synthesising correlations between global range sizes of 7635 species and local species counts collected across 16,562,995 eBird checklists (resulting in 16,562,995 Zr values and corresponding sampling variances; Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data analyzed in the study.

claim: The meta-analysis included 7635 bird species.
source: First, we carry out the largest known meta-analysis by synthesising correlations between global range sizes of 7635 species and local species counts collected across 16,562,995 eBird checklists (resulting in 16,562,995 Zr values and corresponding sampling variances; Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of species included in the analysis.

claim: The study conducted a phylogenetically controlled comparative analysis regressing species range sizes on 7464 estimates of globally derived species' mean density.
source: Second, we conduct a phylogenetically controlled comparative analysis, regressing species range sizes on 7464 estimates of globally derived species' mean density, equivalent to mean local density (per 5-degree grid cell), estimated in earlier work (Callaghan et al., 2021) (see Materials and methods for more details).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phylogenetic analysis conducted in the study.

claim: The overall relationship between local abundance and global occupancy was near-zero (r=0.015).
source: Surprisingly, the overall (aggregated) relationship between local abundance and global occupancy was near-zero (r=0.015), although this relationship was statistically significant due to our extremely large sample size (p=0.0005, z=2.805, Zr = b[overall mean]=0.015, 95% confidence interval, CI = [0.004, 0.025]; Figure 2, Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the eBird data.

claim: The relationship between local abundance and global occupancy was statistically significant (p=0.0005) due to the extremely large sample size.
source: Surprisingly, the overall (aggregated) relationship between local abundance and global occupancy was near-zero (r=0.015), although this relationship was statistically significant due to our extremely large sample size (p=0.0005, z=2.805, Zr = b[overall mean]=0.015, 95% confidence interval, CI = [0.004, 0.025]; Figure 2, Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing significance despite a near-zero effect.

claim: The significant relationship between local abundance and global occupancy disappeared (r=0.0009) once species number and effort time were controlled for.
source: However, this significant relationship disappeared (r=0.0009) once we controlled for species number and effort time (p=0.863, z=0.173, Zr = b[overall mean]=0.0009, 95% CI = [–0.0092, 0.0111]); both variables were statistically significant predictors of the effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis controlling for confounding variables.

claim: Species number and effort time were statistically significant predictors of the AOR effect.
source: However, this significant relationship disappeared (r=0.0009) once we controlled for species number and effort time (p=0.863, z=0.173, Zr = b[overall mean]=0.0009, 95% CI = [–0.0092, 0.0111]); both variables were statistically significant predictors of the effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing these variables as significant predictors.

claim: Increases in species number decreased the strength of the AOR relationship.
source: As expected, the increase in species number (modelled as the inverse of species number – 3, which is equivalent to sampling error for Zr) and effort time on the natural log scale decreased the strength of the relationship (sampling variance: p<0.0001, z=140.29; b[sampling variance]=0.0147, 95% CI = [–0.0149, –0.0145]); ln(effort time): p<0.0001, z=–183.45, b[ln(effort time)]=0.230, 95% CI = [0.226, 0.233]; marginal R2=5.1% for the model with these two predictors; Nakagawa and Schielzeth, 2013; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing the effect of species number.

claim: Increases in effort time decreased the strength of the AOR relationship.
source: As expected, the increase in species number (modelled as the inverse of species number – 3, which is equivalent to sampling error for Zr) and effort time on the natural log scale decreased the strength of the relationship (sampling variance: p<0.0001, z=140.29; b[sampling variance]=0.0147, 95% CI = [–0.0149, –0.0145]); ln(effort time): p<0.0001, z=–183.45, b[ln(effort time)]=0.230, 95% CI = [0.226, 0.233]; marginal R2=5.1% for the model with these two predictors; Nakagawa and Schielzeth, 2013; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing the effect of effort time.

claim: The observations are consistent with the explanation that sampling protocols can create positive artefactual relationships between range and abundance.
source: These observations are consistent with the explanation that sampling protocols can create positive artefactual relationships between range and abundance.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the statistical results showing effects of sampling variables.

claim: The relative heterogeneity (I2[total]) was 13.5%, meaning 86.5% of all observed variation is due to sampling error.
source: A measure of relative heterogeneity I2[total] was 13.5%, meaning that 86.5% of all the observed variation (in Figure 2) is due to sampling error, therefore, is neither biological nor ecological (country level; I2=5.5%, σ2=0.005; state level: I2=6.3%, σ2=0.005; effect-size level; I2=1.5%, σ2=0.001); in contrast, the average I2[total] across 86 ecological meta-analyses was approximately 92% (Senior et al., 2016), making our observed heterogeneity unusually low.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of heterogeneity in the meta-analysis.

claim: The average I2[total] across 86 ecological meta-analyses was approximately 92%.
source: A measure of relative heterogeneity I2[total] was 13.5%, meaning that 86.5% of all the observed variation (in Figure 2) is due to sampling error, therefore, is neither biological nor ecological (country level; I2=5.5%, σ2=0.005; state level: I2=6.3%, σ2=0.005; effect-size level; I2=1.5%, σ2=0.001); in contrast, the average I2[total] across 86 ecological meta-analyses was approximately 92% (Senior et al., 2016), making our observed heterogeneity unusually low.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study comparing heterogeneity across meta-analyses.

claim: The observed heterogeneity in the study was unusually low compared to typical ecological meta-analyses.
source: A measure of relative heterogeneity I2[total] was 13.5%, meaning that 86.5% of all the observed variation (in Figure 2) is due to sampling error, therefore, is neither biological nor ecological (country level; I2=5.5%, σ2=0.005; state level: I2=6.3%, σ2=0.005; effect-size level; I2=1.5%, σ2=0.001); in contrast, the average I2[total] across 86 ecological meta-analyses was approximately 92% (Senior et al., 2016), making our observed heterogeneity unusually low.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the study's heterogeneity to published values from other meta-analyses.

claim: The absolute heterogeneity (σ2[total]=0.011) was approximately one-thirtieth of the heterogeneity found in the previous meta-analysis (σ2[total]=0.323).
source: We found the absolute heterogeneity, σ2[total]=0.011, approximately one-thirtieth of the heterogeneity (σ2[total]=0.323) found in the previous meta-analysis (Blackburn et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of heterogeneity values between the current study and a previous meta-analysis.

claim: The absolute heterogeneity (σ2[total]=0.011) is around one-tenth of the average heterogeneity (σ2[total]=0.125) found in 31 meta-analyses in ecology and evolution.
source: Also, this is around one-tenth of the average heterogeneity (σ2[total]=0.125; median = 0.105) found in 31 meta-analyses in ecology and evolution (Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to published heterogeneity values from other meta-analyses.

claim: Low relative and absolute heterogeneities indicate that the dataset does not have much variability left to be explained.
source: Overall, low relative and absolute heterogeneities indicate that our dataset of 16,562,995 effect sizes does not have much variability left to be explained despite our observations coming from many different locations across the globe and contributed by tens of thousands of individual birdwatchers.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the heterogeneity statistics.

claim: The combination of zero effect and very small heterogeneity is only expected when a particular phenomenon is not real.
source: Importantly, we emphasise that this combination of zero effect and very small heterogeneity is only expected when a particular phenomenon is not real.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about what statistical patterns indicate about the reality of a phenomenon.

claim: The phylogenetic comparative analysis showed that global range sizes had little predictive power on mean species density (p=0.808, t99.6 = 0.0227, b[slope]=0.0928, 95% CI = [–0.1615, 0.2068]).
source: Moreover, our phylogenetic comparative analysis, which accounted for phylogenetic uncertainty (Nakagawa and De Villemereuil, 2019), corroborated our meta-analytic results (cf. Gaston et al., 1997a). The global range sizes had little predictive power on mean species density (both on log10; p=0.808, t99.6 = 0.0227, b[slope]=0.0928, 95% CI = [–0.1615, 0.2068]; Figure 3, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis from the phylogenetic comparative analysis.

claim: The results provide overwhelming evidence against the fundamental relationship between species range and local abundance.
source: Taken together, our results provide overwhelming evidence against the fundamental relationship between species range and local abundance, while the results are consistent with this relationship as a sampling artefact.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined results of the meta-analysis and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The results are consistent with the AOR relationship being a sampling artefact.
source: Taken together, our results provide overwhelming evidence against the fundamental relationship between species range and local abundance, while the results are consistent with this relationship as a sampling artefact.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the statistical results showing effects of sampling variables.

claim: Relationships between global species ranges and local counts can be null, strongly negative, or strongly positive, generated primarily by sampling variance.
source: Nevertheless, our results are also consistent with previously published empirical evidence. This is because we have shown that relationships between global species ranges and local counts can be null, strongly negative, or strongly positive, which can be generated primarily by sampling (error) variance (shown in Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2 and inference from the analysis.

claim: Fishing quotas, conservation priorities, and invasive species control strategies based on AORs must be reconsidered.
source: Our results demonstrate clearly that the AOR is not observed in a very large global dataset, with both applied and theoretical ramifications. First, we must reconsider fishing quotas, conservation priorities, and invasive species control strategies based on AORs (cf. Gaston, 1999a).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the study's findings about the non-existence of AOR.

claim: It may be futile to pursue all ecological or biological mechanisms proposed for AORs.
source: Second, it may be futile to pursue all ecological or biological mechanisms proposed for AORs (see Gaston et al., 1997b; Borregaard and Rahbek, 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the study's findings about the non-existence of AOR.

claim: The spatial neutral model is not a suitable null model of macroecology.
source: Most notably, our near-zero results with small heterogeneity suggest that contrary to earlier suggestions (Bell, 2001; Hubbell, 1997), the spatial neutral model is not a suitable null model of macroecology.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the study's findings contradicting predictions of neutral theory.

claim: If local adaptation were to disrupt a predicted positive AOR relationship, substantial heterogeneity and a reduced relationship would be observed, not a near-zero relationship.
source: Within the neutral theoretical framework, AORs can be broken by local adaptation (an alternative hypothesis) (Bell, 2001). If local adaptation were to disrupt a predicted positive relationship (AOR), we would have observed substantial heterogeneity and a reduced relationship, not a near-zero relationship.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about what patterns would be expected under local adaptation.

claim: It is extremely unlikely that local adaptation and neutral processes are in a perfect balance, resulting in an exact-zero relationship with little heterogeneity.
source: This is because it is extremely unlikely that local adaptation and neutral processes are in a perfect balance, resulting in an exact-zero relationship with little heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the improbability of perfect balance between opposing processes.

claim: Local adaptations are expected to create local specificities and global variability/heterogeneity.
source: In other words, local adaptations are expected to create local specificities and global variability/heterogeneity; our meta-analysis did not find such variability.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the expected consequences of local adaptation.

claim: Any model of a positive AOR posits a mechanism that connects species range and local abundance.
source: We point out that any model of a positive AOR posits a mechanism that connects species range and local abundance on the one hand.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the nature of AOR models.

claim: Rabinowitz effectively decoupled species range and local abundance.
source: Rabinowitz, on the other hand, effectively decoupled these two variables (Rabinowitz, 1981), although studies using her framework found positive correlations between species range and local abundance (Yu and Dobson, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rabinowitz's work.

claim: Studies using Rabinowitz's framework found positive correlations between species range and local abundance.
source: Rabinowitz, on the other hand, effectively decoupled these two variables (Rabinowitz, 1981), although studies using her framework found positive correlations between species range and local abundance (Yu and Dobson, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study using Rabinowitz's framework.

claim: Rabinowitz suggests seven forms of rarity by adding habitat specificity to species range and abundance.
source: By adding habit specificity to species range and abundance, she suggests seven forms of rarity, which could reflect different underlying macroecological mechanisms; e.g., two forms of rarity are geographically restricted but locally abundant with narrow or broad habitat types.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of Rabinowitz's framework as discussed in the text.

claim: The study's results support the existence of many 'rare' species as defined by Rabinowitz's framework.
source: Unlike the world created by the spatial neutral model, our results support many such 'rare' species (Yu and Dobson, 2000).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the study's findings in relation to Rabinowitz's framework.

claim: Rabinowitz's framework has more empirical support from global-scale patterns of species abundance than the AOR.
source: Therefore, we believe Rabinowitz's framework, rather than the AOR, has more empirical support from global-scale patterns of species abundance and provides a useful conceptual structure for future theoretical and applied work, although this line of work is still limited.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the study's findings and comparison to Rabinowitz's framework.

claim: The study only deals with interspecific AORs among birds.
source: Although our findings challenge some long-held assumptions about the consistency of the AOR, our work only deals with interspecific AORs among birds, synthesising observations from potentially heterogeneous locations, ecological contexts, and data quality.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the scope of the study.

claim: The study did not account for anthropogenic changes in populations or range sizes.
source: We further acknowledge that we did not account for anthropogenic changes in populations or range sizes in our analyses and, therefore, we included alien species without separating them from native ones.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a limitation of the study.

claim: The study included alien species without separating them from native ones.
source: We further acknowledge that we did not account for anthropogenic changes in populations or range sizes in our analyses and, therefore, we included alien species without separating them from native ones.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study's methodology.

claim: Species range data are often overestimated due to the failure to capture gaps in actual distributions.
source: More precise range-size estimates would also improve the accuracy of AOR assessments since species range data are often overestimated due to the failure to capture gaps in actual distributions (Ocampo-Peñuela et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on range size estimation.

claim: Much of the overestimation in the previous meta-analysis originates from publication bias and confirmation bias.
source: However, we speculate that much of the overestimation originates from publication bias and confirmation bias, which is supported by mounting evidence from meta-research studies (Holman et al., 2015; van Wilgenburg and Elgar, 2013; Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is speculative but supported by citations to meta-research studies on bias.

claim: eBird datasets are free from publication and confirmation biases.
source: Although we do not have direct evidence, our eBird datasets are free from these two types of biases (i.e. birdwatchers generally do not think of the macroecological patterns that would later be tested with the data they submit), while the literature-based meta-analyses are not.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the nature of citizen science data collection.

claim: The original meta-analysis of AOR stated that more than half a million unpublished null results would be required to nullify the effect.
source: Regarding publication bias, the original meta-analysis of AOR states, 'the fail-safe number indicates that more than half a million unpublished null results would be required to nullify an effect of this magnitude' (Blackburn et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a direct quote from the previous meta-analysis.

claim: The study provided much more than half a million null effects to reach a null conclusion.
source: Indeed, we provided much more than half a million null effects to reach our null conclusion (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is based on the data presented in the study.

claim: A recent study re-examining 86 ecological and evolutionary meta-analyses demonstrated a 23% reduction in overall effects due to publication bias.
source: A recent study re-examining 86 ecological and evolutionary meta-analyses demonstrated a 23% reduction in overall effects due to publication bias, turning 33 of 50 statistically significant meta-analytic conclusions (66%) into non-significant (Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a meta-research study.

claim: A study examining 83 topics in life sciences showed that the effect size of non-blind studies was twice as large as blinded counterparts.
source: Similarly, a study examining 83 topics in life sciences showed that the effect size of non-blind studies, which are at risk of confirmation bias, was twice as large as blinded counterparts protected against confirmation bias (Holman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a meta-research study on confirmation bias.

claim: Meta-research on behavioural ecology identified 79 studies on nestmate recognition, 23 of which were conducted blind.
source: Meta-research on behavioural ecology identified 79 studies on nestmate recognition, 23 of which were conducted blind (van Wilgenburg and Elgar, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a meta-research study.

claim: Non-blind studies confirmed a hypothesis of no aggression towards nestmates nearly three times more often than blind studies.
source: Non-blind studies confirmed a hypothesis of no aggression towards nestmates nearly three times more often.
evidence: This claim is based on the meta-research study cited in the previous sentence.

claim: There have been over 100 studies on ego depletion in psychology.
source: There have been over 100 studies, and many theoretical models support the hypothesis of 'ego depletion', where self-control is a finite resource, so self-control will decrease once it is exerted (Inzlicht and Schmeichel, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review of ego depletion research.

claim: The first meta-analysis of ego depletion suggested very strong support for it (d=0.62).
source: The first meta-analysis of ego depletion, like AOR, suggested very strong support for it (standardised mean difference, or d=0.62).
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the ego depletion literature discussed in the text.

claim: A subsequent multi-lab replication found that ego depletion does not exist and is so weak as to be negligible (d=0.04).
source: Yet, a subsequent multi-lab replication found that ego depletion does not exist and is so weak as to be negligible (d=0.04) (Hagger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a multi-lab replication study.

claim: A series of multi-lab replications has indicated that several psychological phenomena once believed to be real are too weak to be useful or are non-existent.
source: Indeed, a series of multi-lab replications has indicated that several psychological phenomena, which were once believed to be real beyond a reasonable doubt, are too weak to be useful or are non-existent (Kvarven et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on replication in psychology.

claim: Recently collated large datasets collected for non-hypothesis-driven purposes offer a unique opportunity to revisit and retest longstanding ideas in ecology.
source: In ecology, recently collated large datasets collected for non-hypothesis-driven purposes offer a unique opportunity to revisit and retest longstanding ideas.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the potential of large datasets.

claim: Very few ecological topics are free from sampling, confirmation, and publication biases.
source: Taken together, we call for re-examining all ecological laws, rules, and patterns, as very few topics are free from sampling, confirmation, and publication biases (cf. Hughes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from meta-research findings and is supported by a citation.

claim: A credibility revolution in ecology needs to embrace non-traditional methods such as pre-registration, registered reports, prospective and living meta-analyses, open synthesis communities, and big-team-science collaborations.
source: A credibility revolution in ecology, like in psychology, needs to embrace non-traditional methods to avoid confirmation and publication bias, such as pre-registration (Nosek et al., 2018), registered reports (Chambers and Tzavella, 2022), prospective and living meta-analyses, open synthesis communities (Nakagawa et al., 2020), and big-team-science collaborations (Coles et al., 2022) involving community (citizen) scientists (Callaghan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to works describing these methodological approaches.

claim: eBird was launched in 2002 by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology.
source: eBird, launched in 2002 by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, is a global citizen science project that enlists volunteer birdwatchers to submit 'checklists' of birds seen and/or heard while birdwatching.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the history of eBird.

claim: eBird data undergo a semi-automated filtering process before being entered into the dataset.
source: Data undergo a semi-automated filtering process before being entered into the dataset, and expert reviewers additionally review species (or counts of species) that surpass preset filters before being accepted into the dataset (Gilfedder et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation describing eBird's data quality procedures.

claim: The study downloaded the eBird basic dataset version ebd_rel-May2020.
source: We downloaded the eBird basic dataset (version ebd_rel-May2020) and considered all eBird checklists between 1 January 2005 and 31 May 2020.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data source used in the study.

claim: The study considered all eBird checklists between 1 January 2005 and 31 May 2020.
source: We downloaded the eBird basic dataset (version ebd_rel-May2020) and considered all eBird checklists between 1 January 2005 and 31 May 2020.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the temporal scope of the data.

claim: The study only included complete checklists.
source: We only included: (1) complete checklists; (2) checklists that were <240 min and >5 min; (3) checklists that travelled <5 km; and (4) checklists that travelled <500 ha.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data filtering criteria.

claim: The study only included checklists that were less than 240 minutes and greater than 5 minutes.
source: We only included: (1) complete checklists; (2) checklists that were <240 min and >5 min; (3) checklists that travelled <5 km; and (4) checklists that travelled <500 ha.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data filtering criteria.

claim: The study excluded any checklist that had at least an 'X' on it.
source: Because birdwatchers will sometimes use an 'X' to signify presence, and this is most likely to happen for more abundant species, we excluded any checklist that had at least an 'X' on it, as this could potentially influence the correlation between the abundance of a species and range size by disproportionately removing the most abundant species from the correlation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data filtering criteria and the reasoning behind it.

claim: The study only considered checklists that had at least 10 species recorded on them.
source: We further only considered checklists that had at least 10 species recorded on them, and a correlation test was performed only if we had range size data (see below) for a minimum of four species on the checklist.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data filtering criteria.

claim: The study used range size maps from BirdLife International, 2023.
source: We used range size maps from BirdLife International, 2023, using their global range, ignoring the differences between resident and breeding ranges.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data source for range sizes.

claim: The study obtained 16,562,995 correlations based on 3,005,668,285 individual bird observations.
source: We obtained 16,562,995 correlations based on 3,005,668,285 individual bird observations, including 7635 species.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the scale of the data analyzed.

claim: The study transformed correlations into Fisher's Z (Zr) to unbound and calculated sampling variance for each Zr value.
source: We transformed correlations between species abundance and range into Fisher's Z or Zr to unbound and calculated sampling variance for each Zr value; note that the inverse of the sampling variance of Zr is N (the number of species in a checklist) – 3 (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical methods used.

claim: The inverse of the sampling variance of Zr is N (the number of species in a checklist) – 3.
source: We transformed correlations between species abundance and range into Fisher's Z or Zr to unbound and calculated sampling variance for each Zr value; note that the inverse of the sampling variance of Zr is N (the number of species in a checklist) – 3 (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is a statement about a statistical property of Fisher's Z transformation.

claim: The study used the R package asreml to run a multilevel random effects model.
source: We used the R package, asreml (Nakagawa and Santos, 2012), to run a multilevel random effects model (Nakagawa and Santos, 2012); note that asreml is a commercial package, so it is not free.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical software used.

claim: The study had 'country' (245 levels) and state code (2871 levels) as random factors in the model.
source: We had 'country' (245 levels) and state code (2871 levels) as random factors in the model to control for non-independence.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model structure.

claim: The study used data from a recently published analysis of global abundances for birds within 5-degree grid cells for the macro-scale analysis.
source: For this, we used data from a recently published analysis of global abundances for birds within 5-degree grid cells (Callaghan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data source for the macro-scale analysis.

claim: The macro-scale analysis incorporated a total of 7464 bird species.
source: Our analysis incorporated a total of 7464 species of bird species, corresponding to the species for which we had both range maps and estimated density, along with phylogenetic information included in Jetz et al., 2012.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of species in the macro-scale analysis.

claim: The study used avian phylogeny from Jetz et al., 2012.
source: We used avian phylogeny from Jetz et al., 2012, and analysed 100 phylogenetic trees using the R function phylolm (Ho and Ané, 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phylogenetic data source.

claim: The study analyzed 100 phylogenetic trees using the R function phylolm.
source: We used avian phylogeny from Jetz et al., 2012, and analysed 100 phylogenetic trees using the R function phylolm (Ho and Ané, 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phylogenetic analysis method.

claim: The meta-analysis is based on approximately 3 billion bird observations.
source: Yet, based on the largest known meta-analysis of 16,562,995 correlations from ~3 billion bird observations, this relationship was indistinguishable from zero.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the scale of the data in the abstract.

claim: In the phylogenetic comparative analysis, species range had no predictive power over the global mean abundance of 7464 bird species.
source: Further, in a phylogenetic comparative analysis, species range had no predictive power over the global mean abundance of 7464 bird species.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of the phylogenetic analysis in the abstract.

claim: Publication and confirmation biases may have created AORs, an illusion of a 'universal' pattern.
source: We suggest that publication and confirmation biases may have created AORs, an illusion of a 'universal' pattern.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the study's findings and meta-research on bias.

claim: The nullification of AOR highlights the need for ecologists to instigate a credibility revolution like psychology.
source: This nullification highlights the need for ecologists to instigate a credibility revolution like psychology, where many classic phenomena have been nullified.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on inference from the study's findings and parallels with psychology.

claim: Many classic phenomena in psychology have been nullified.
source: This nullification highlights the need for ecologists to instigate a credibility revolution like psychology, where many classic phenomena have been nullified.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the replication crisis in psychology.

claim: The relationship between local abundance and global occupancy was r=0.015 with a 95% confidence interval of [0.004, 0.025].
source: Surprisingly, the overall (aggregated) relationship between local abundance and global occupancy was near-zero (r=0.015), although this relationship was statistically significant due to our extremely large sample size (p=0.0005, z=2.805, Zr = b[overall mean]=0.015, 95% confidence interval, CI = [0.004, 0.025]; Figure 2, Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical results.

claim: After controlling for species number and effort time, the relationship between local abundance and global occupancy was r=0.0009 with a 95% CI of [–0.0092, 0.0111].
source: However, this significant relationship disappeared (r=0.0009) once we controlled for species number and effort time (p=0.863, z=0.173, Zr = b[overall mean]=0.0009, 95% CI = [–0.0092, 0.0111]); both variables were statistically significant predictors of the effect.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical results after controlling for confounders.

claim: The marginal R2 was 5.1% for the model with species number and effort time as predictors.
source: As expected, the increase in species number (modelled as the inverse of species number – 3, which is equivalent to sampling error for Zr) and effort time on the natural log scale decreased the strength of the relationship (sampling variance: p<0.0001, z=140.29; b[sampling variance]=0.0147, 95% CI = [–0.0149, –0.0145]); ln(effort time): p<0.0001, z=–183.45, b[ln(effort time)]=0.230, 95% CI = [0.226, 0.233]; marginal R2=5.1% for the model with these two predictors; Nakagawa and Schielzeth, 2013; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model fit statistic.

claim: The previous meta-analysis for birds found r=0.74 or Zr = 0.95.
source: Given the different potential biases mentioned before, we expected a more modest relationship in relation to that of the previous meta-analysis (r=0.58; note that this relationship included many different taxa; if restricted to bird species, it was even stronger r=0.74 or Zr = 0.95) (Blackburn and Gaston, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the previous meta-analysis.
